title: Beyond the Pitch: How Women Are Redefining World Cup Fandom
summary: Amid the roaring, male-dominated crowds of the 2026 World Cup, NPR's Jasmine Garsd found a quieter but equally passionate expression of fandom: intricate soccer-themed nail art. In Houston, she visited salons where women spent hours getting flags, trophies, and player numbers painted on their fingertips, all while debating fútbol. But the deeper story emerged in conversations with women who've fought to claim their place in the sport. Zhraa Hamidy, 22, fell in love with soccer early and earned a college scholarship—only to have her father forbid her from playing, saying it wasn't for women. Now, she coaches Michigan FC, a girls' team primarily composed of young Muslim athletes. Her star player, 16-year-old Fatima Alzahraa Yazdchi, stunned onlookers with aggressive dribbling and dreams of her own scholarship. When Garsd asked Fatima about her favorite goal, she didn't cite a professional—she described her own: a 40-yard strike after a painful foul, sailing over the goalie's hands. Garsd's own history mirrors this resilience. Growing up in Argentina, she played obsessively with neighborhood boys until her father, too, declared soccer no place for girls. She rebelled, eventually channeling her love into journalism—covering Lionel Messi's rise and now the World Cup. "Soccer's soul lives in the neighborhood pitch," she writes, "where girls and boys dream big, and celebrate goals as if it were them, playing on the world stage." The 2026 tournament has faced controversies, but for Garsd, the enduring image is of women—on the field and in the salon—reclaiming the beautiful game.
why_it_matters: For middle-schoolers who might feel a sport 'isn't for them,' these stories prove that passion and perseverance can break down old rules. They show that fandom takes many forms—and that reclaiming a space can change who gets to play, coach, and dream.

background_read: The 2026 FIFA World Cup, the first men's tournament with 48 teams, is being co-hosted by the United States, Canada, and Mexico, drawing global attention to North American soccer culture—but also reigniting debates about who truly belongs in the sport.

Historically, women were barred from playing organized football in many countries; even after bans lifted, cultural resistance kept countless girls off the pitch. Jasmine Garsd's own experience in Argentina, where her father told her soccer was not for girls, mirrors those wider patterns.
Michigan FC, a youth club coached by Hamidy, serves primarily young Muslim athletes—a demographic often underrepresented in U.S. soccer—showing how grassroots teams are changing the face of the game.
The nail art described in the salons is more than decoration: it represents a parallel fandom space where women debate the sport and display their passion when stadium crowds can feel unwelcoming.

Such expressions of women's fandom challenge the old assumption that being a 'real fan' means only shouting in the stands, and they connect to a larger movement for gender equality in sports that has gained momentum since the 1999 Women's World Cup.

perspectives.description: Hamidy and Fatima demonstrate that young women can excel in soccer, earn scholarships, and become coaches even when families initially resist—lighting a path for girls who face similar barriers.

Skeptics note that the World Cup's massive corporate focus can overshadow grassroots programs, making it harder for low-income girls to access the same quality coaching and facilities that help talents like Fatima emerge.

Researchers point out that women's fandom often takes alternative shapes—like nail art and salon debates—because traditional stadium culture can feel alienating, yet these spaces are just as authentic and passionate.

The 2026 tournament could push more investment into women's and girls' programs, especially if players like Fatima gain visibility; however, real change depends on whether institutions keep their promises long after the World Cup cameras leave.
